description:
Buscamos desarrollar una herramienta interactiva que nos permita explorar Marte integrando la información de diferentes misiones para poder hacer el terreno visible, identificar posibles peligros, determinar rutas y descubrir oportunidades de investigación.

Buscamos personas interesadas en la tecnología, la ciencia, la programación, la IA, la cartografía y la exploración espacial. Valoramos la curiosidad, la iniciativa, el compromiso, el trabajo en equipo, las ganas de aprender.
summary:
CANIS MAJOR 13 transforms orbital data from a sector of Jezero Crater into a reproducible topographic exploration experience, revealing how terrain measurements change between scenarios and where the limits of the available data affect their interpretation.
Our web application integrates CTX orbital imagery, a digital terrain model (DTM), historical Perseverance rover positions, and four documented surface photographs. Users compare a straight-line reference (Scenario A) with a user-drawn path (Scenario B) connecting the same endpoints.
Elevation profiles displayed on a common scale, horizontal distances, cumulative elevation gain and loss, and missing-data indicators make these differences explicit and understandable.
Through an interactive Martian map, CANIS connects orbital terrain information with surface-level mission context. It provides a transparent way to examine assumptions, compare hypothetical scenarios, and explain results using traceable scientific sources.
CANIS supports preliminary terrain interpretation rather than operational route planning. Explainable terrain characterization is the next stage of development we propose.
details:
What does your project do, and how does it work?

CANIS MAJOR 13 is an interactive web application designed to explore and understand the Martian terrain using real NASA scientific data.

It focuses on a 915.6 km² sector of Jezero Crater, integrating CTX orbital imagery, a digital terrain model (DTM), 708 historical Perseverance rover positions, and four documented surface observations.

Its core feature compares two hypothetical paths connecting the same starting point and destination: a straight-line reference (Scenario A) and a user-drawn alternative (Scenario B). CANIS calculates and displays differences in horizontal distance, elevation profiles, cumulative ascent, and descent.

What benefits does your project provide?

CANIS makes complex scientific terrain data easier to explore and understand through an interactive visual experience. It helps users examine how topographic measurements vary between different paths while recognizing the limitations of the available data.

What is the expected impact of your project?

CANIS makes scientific information more accessible to students, researchers, and people interested in planetary exploration.

Its initial applications are educational and technical, with the potential to support future research and the development of more advanced tools for exploring Martian terrain.

What tools, programming languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

We developed the platform using React, TypeScript, Leaflet, and Vite, with Python and GDAL for geospatial data preparation and verification.

The final validated version passed 75 automated tests.

What makes your project creative?

CANIS brings together orbital imagery, terrain elevation data, rover history, and documented surface observations in a unified interactive platform.

Rather than simply displaying a Martian map, it enables users to compare hypothetical paths through reproducible topographic analysis, connecting orbital-scale terrain information with real mission observations.

What factors did your team consider?

We prioritized scientific data provenance, reproducible processing methods, terrain resolution, data quality, and transparency about the limitations of the available information.

CANIS supports preliminary terrain interpretation and comparison of hypothetical scenarios, rather than operational route planning or safety assessment.

As our next development stage, we propose explainable terrain characterization and zoning. Future possibilities include automated route alternatives and AI-assisted explanatory tools.
